question: What is the main goal of doing a thoracentesis?

options.A: To clear mucus plugs from the main airways
options.B: To measure pressure inside the right atrium
options.C: To deliver medications directly into the lung tissue
options.D: To remove fluid or air from the pleural space

explanation: You've got this! A thoracentesis simply means putting a tiny needle into the chest cavity to drain out unwanted fluid or air that shouldn't be there. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T17#GNS213_U2_T17_h1)

question: Why would a doctor order a diagnostic thoracentesis?

options.A: To measure how much oxygen the lungs can hold total
options.B: To find out the exact cause of a pleural fluid buildup
options.C: To prevent the development of a future heart attack
options.D: To permanently cure chronic obstructive pulmonary disease

explanation: Great thinking! When we take a little sample of that fluid to the lab, we can figure out why it started gathering in the chest in the first place. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T17#GNS213_U2_T17_h1)

question: Where is the pleural space actually located in the body?

options.A: Between the visceral pleura and the parietal pleura
options.B: Directly inside the chambers of the human heart
options.C: Between the skin and the outer rib cage muscles
options.D: Inside the main bronchial tubes of the lungs

explanation: Spot on! It sits neatly as a tiny space between the two membrane layers that wrap around and protect our lungs. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T17#GNS213_U2_T17_h2)

question: When doing a thoracentesis, where should the needle enter the chest to keep blood vessels and nerves safe?

options.A: Directly through the middle of the rib bone
options.B: Right beneath the bottom edge of the upper rib
options.C: Over the upper border of the lower rib
options.D: Through the soft center of the sternum bone

explanation: You're doing great! Nerves and blood vessels love to hide right under the bottom edge of each rib, so we slide the needle just over the top edge of the lower rib to avoid them. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T17#GNS213_U2_T17_h2)

question: What is the best position for your patient during a thoracentesis?

options.A: Lying flat on the back with arms raised above the head
options.B: Sitting upright and leaning forward over a bedside table
options.C: Positioned flat on the unaffected side with knees bent
options.D: Prone with a pillow placed directly under the abdomen

explanation: Awesome! This forward-leaning posture opens up the spaces between the ribs nicely, making it much safer and easier for the doctor to reach the fluid. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T17#GNS213_U2_T17_h3)

question: As a smart nurse, which lab result must you check before a patient has a thoracentesis?
explanation: Brilliant! Always check clotting times and platelets first so you know the patient won't run into any heavy bleeding issues during the procedure. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T17#GNS213_U2_T17_h3)

question: What is your main job as the nurse while the doctor performs a thoracentesis?

options.A: Reading the final lab results before fluid collection
options.B: Inserting the drainage catheter into the pleural cavity
options.C: Administering general anesthesia through an IV line
options.D: Monitoring vital signs and watching for signs of distress

explanation: Exactly right! Your eyes are on the patient—keep a close check on their breathing, heart rate, and comfort while the fluid drains. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T17#GNS213_U2_T17_h4)

question: Your patient suddenly gasps and feels dizzy halfway through draining fluid. What should you do first?

options.A: Document the total amount of fluid drained so far
options.B: Notify the provider immediately and stop the drainage
options.C: Administer the prescribed oral pain medication right away
options.D: Ask the patient to sit up straight and take deep breaths

explanation: Safety first! Sudden dizziness or coughing can mean a rapid fluid shift or a lung issue, so pause the procedure and alert the doctor right away. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T17#GNS213_U2_T17_h4)

question: Why is a chest X-ray usually done right after a thoracentesis?

options.A: To measure the exact volume of remaining chest fluid
options.B: To check if the rib bones healed from the puncture
options.C: To confirm lung expansion and check for a collapsed lung
options.D: To verify that the heart valves are working normally

explanation: Spot on! An X-ray lets us double-check that the lung expanded nicely and that no air slipped into the chest cavity. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T17#GNS213_U2_T17_h5)

question: How should you position your patient right after a thoracentesis is finished?
explanation: You nailed it! Having them lie on the good (unaffected) side helps the tiny puncture site seal up and lets the treated lung expand fully. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T17#GNS213_U2_T17_h5)

question: What is a classic sign that a patient developed a pneumothorax after a thoracentesis?

options.A: Swelling and redness around the patient's ankles
options.B: Sudden severe pain radiating down the left arm
options.C: Sudden shortness of breath and absent breath sounds on one side
options.D: A high fever with productive green sputum and chills

explanation: Great clinical eye! If air leaks into the chest, it causes the lung to pull away, leading to sudden trouble breathing and quiet breath sounds on that side. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T17#GNS213_U2_T17_h6)

question: What causes re-expansion pulmonary edema during chest fluid drainage?

options.A: Removing a large volume of fluid too quickly
options.B: Using a needle that is too wide for the intercostal space
options.C: Failing to give the patient local anesthetic before starting
options.D: Positioning the patient on the wrong side afterward

explanation: You've got this! Draining too much fluid too fast places sudden stress on the lung blood vessels, causing fluid to seep into the tiny air sacs. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T17#GNS213_U2_T17_h6)
